To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the set-up error in image-guided radio-therapy can be reduced using a CBCT imaging system compared with the use of planar imaging systems.
the planning margins for prostate and head and neck cancer are larger in CBCT than in portal imaging and that the planning margins are larger for prostate cancer than for head and neck cancer.

1) the set-up error is significantly reduced by image-guided radio-therapy (IGRT) compared to conventional radiotherapy; 2) the set-up errors for the different imaging systems are similar; 3) the planning margin can be reduced by IGRT; 4) the planning margin is larger in prostate than in head-and-neck cancer, and; 5) the planning margins for the different imaging modalities are similar.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new method of radiotherapy planning for prostate cancer.
the development of a system that can be used to detect the presence of a person in a room.
the development of a system for the automatic detection of the tumor in the CT images of the patient and its subsequent use in the treatment of the patient.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are no significant differences between 2D, planar, 2D/3D, and volumetric IGRT systems in terms of set-up errors or planning margins for prostate and head and neck cancer.
the use of CBCT in prostate cancer patients does not improve the accuracy of prostate radiotherapy.
the use of CBCT for IGRT of prostate cancer patients in this setting does not seem to be beneficial in terms of setup errors, but the use of CBRT for prostate cancer patients does.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of a 3-D image-guided radiation therapy system (IGRT) is feasible and safe, and that the use of IGRT is likely to improve the accuracy and precision of radiation treatment.
it is not possible to accurately predict the dose delivered to the prostate gland based on a single CT scan.
the use of CBCT for prostate cancer is not yet justified, but that it may have a role for head and neck cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current practice of using a 2.5 cm margin in the lateral direction in prostate radiotherapy is likely to be overestimated.
the current imaging systems for IGRT, including the CBCT, are not sufficiently accurate to provide the required planning margin.
the planning margins are smaller for CBCT-based IGRT than for kV-IGRT and MV-IGRT.
